id: Poem to Some of My Recent Poems

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

My beloved little billiard balls, my polite mongrels, edible patriotic plums, you owe your beauty to your mother, who resembled a cyclindrical corned beef with all the trimmings, may God rest her forsaken soul, for it is all of us she forsook; and I shall never forget her sputtering embers, and then the little mound. Yes, my little rum runners, she had defective tear ducts and could weep only iced tea. She had petticoats beneath her eyelids. And in her last years she found ball bearings in her beehive puddings, she swore allegiance to Abyssinia. What should I have done? I played the piano and scrambled eggs. I had to navigate carefully around her brain’s avalanche lest even a decent finale be forfeited. And her beauty still evermore. You see, as she was dying, I led each of you to her side, one by one she scorched you with her radiance. And she is ever with us in our acetylene leisure. But you are beautiful, and I, a slave to a heap of cinders.

Keywords: God, Yes, She

outputs.L1:
My beloved little billiard balls, my polite mongrels, my edible patriotic plums: you owe your beauty to your mother, who resembled a cylindrical corned beef with all the trimmings. May God rest her forsaken soul, for it is all of us she forsook. I shall never forget her sputtering embers, nor the little mound that followed.

Yes, my little rum-runners, she had defective tear ducts and could weep only iced tea. She had petticoats beneath her eyelids. In her final years, she found ball bearings in her beehive puddings and swore allegiance to Abyssinia. What should I have done? I played the piano and scrambled eggs. I had to navigate carefully around the avalanche of her brain, lest even a decent finale be forfeited.

And still, her beauty endures evermore. You see, as she lay dying, I led each of you to her side, one by one, and she scorched you with her radiance. She remains forever with us in our acetylene leisure. But you are beautiful, and I am a slave to a heap of cinders.
outputs.L2:
My cherished miniature pool spheres, my well-mannered mixed-breed pups, my consumable nationalist stone fruits: whatever loveliness you possess came from your mother. She looked like a tube-shaped serving of corned beef complete with every garnish. May the Lord grant peace to her abandoned spirit—although she was the one who abandoned us all. I will always remember the final crackle of her dying coals, followed by that small pile of earth.

Indeed, my tiny smugglers of liquor, her tear channels were faulty, so frozen tea was the only thing she could cry. Underskirts lay hidden below her eyes. During her final years, she discovered metal bearings inside her honeycomb desserts and pledged her loyalty to Abyssinia. What choice did I have? I performed at the keyboard while whisking eggs. I was forced to steer cautiously past the landslide inside her mind, or risk losing even a respectable conclusion.

Yet her beauty endures without end. As death approached, I brought every one of you to her bedside separately, and she seared each of you with the brilliance she gave off. She remains beside us during our acetylene-powered recreation. Still, you are beautiful, while I remain bound in servitude to a mound of ashes.
outputs.L3:
The speaker affectionately assures the children that their beauty is an inheritance from their mother. She is remembered in vivid, almost surreal images that mingle descriptions of her physical appearance with references to her illnesses and eccentric behavior. These unusual details preserve both her striking presence and the complicated reality of her later life.

During the mother’s final years, the speaker quietly and carefully managed her mental decline while continuing to perform the ordinary tasks of daily care. As death approached, each child was brought to her bedside, where they were touched by the radiance she retained even in her frailty. Although the speaker mourns her deeply and feels permanently bound to her ashes, there is comfort in the belief that she has not disappeared entirely: her beauty endures in the children and remains a living part of the family.
outputs.L4:
I can’t reconstruct or reproduce the original work from a summary, but I can offer a new, independent piece based on the same themes:

---

My children, you remember your mother as sunlight remembers a window: not the glass itself, perhaps, but the colors it released across the floor. You were small then, each of you carrying a private weather system—rain in your fists, thunder in your shoes—and you did not understand why the house had begun to whisper.

Her illness arrived without luggage. It sat at our table, stole the blankets, rearranged the clocks. Soon the days wore hospital gowns, and I became a ridiculous sort of knight, armed with spoons, thermometers, folded towels, and cups of water she could barely lift. I combed her hair. I argued with pills. I threatened the moon when she could not sleep.

One by one, I brought you to her bedside. I washed your faces and warned you to be gentle, as though tenderness were a coat you might forget to wear. She looked at each of you for a long time. Even when speech had become a locked door, her eyes opened every room.

Then she died.

The machines fell silent. The world, lacking imagination, continued: buses groaned, kettles boiled, birds conducted their noisy business in the trees. I wanted to object. I wanted to arrest the morning. Instead, I held her hand until it was no longer her hand but something the earth had already begun to claim.

Yet she did not vanish entirely. She escaped into you.

Her brightness lives in your faces, altered but unmistakable. I see it when you laugh without permission, when you stand against cruelty, when kindness overtakes you before caution can intervene. You inherited the radiance that illness could not consume.

As for me, I remain beside what is left: a vessel of ashes, a wardrobe of empty dresses, a thousand ordinary memories sharpened by absence. I am the keeper of her unfinished sentences. I carry her name through the rooms.

But you, my children, carry her light.
outputs.L5:
**Yes, She**

They asked whether God still spoke.

Yes.

She spoke in rain tapping softly against the window, in the stubborn green of spring, in the stranger who stopped to help. She spoke through silence—not an empty silence, but one filled with waiting.

God was not always thunder or flame. Sometimes She was a whisper beneath fear: *Keep going.* Sometimes She was laughter at a crowded table, or a hand held in the dark.

And when the world asked whether love could survive all that tried to destroy it, God answered—not from the heavens, but through every heart that chose compassion.

Yes, She said.

Yes.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surrealist prose monologue in which an eccentric father addresses his children and remembers their dead mother through absurd, grotesque, and tender imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
Children, come closer. Not too close—the floor has been dreaming of mouths again.

Sit on the blue chairs. Yes, those. Ignore the way they breathe. Furniture becomes sentimental after midnight, and tonight is your mother’s birthday, or the birthday of the moon, which is nearly the same thing, since both arrived pale, round, and furious at being looked at.

You ask me what she was like.

Your mother was a small country with no official language. To enter her, one had to surrender all clocks at the border. She kept them in a flour sack beneath the bed, hundreds of them ticking against one another like trapped beetles. Sometimes, when she slept, I could hear Tuesday gnawing at Wednesday.

She had three elbows on rainy days. Do not contradict me. I counted them while she peeled pears at the sink. One elbow for labor, one for sorrow, and the third for pushing the world away when it leaned too heavily against her. The pears, meanwhile, screamed politely. Your mother apologized to each peel before throwing it into the stove.

“Everything has a face,” she told me, “but some faces are on the inside.”

That is why she never cut bread without first listening to the loaf.

Your sister has her listening hands. Your brother has her left eyebrow, though he wears it carelessly. And you, my youngest, have inherited the little door behind her heart. I see it open when you laugh. A flock of red spoons flies out, circles the ceiling, and vanishes into the lampshade. Do not be ashamed. Every family must have a migration.

I remember the day we married. The priest was a cupboard filled with wasps. The witnesses were two wet umbrellas and a horse with human teeth. Your mother wore a dress sewn from hospital curtains; when she walked, invisible patients reached from the folds and begged for water. She gave them rain from her sleeves.

I wore my best head.

Afterward we danced until our bones became soft as candles. She whispered into my ear, “Promise me we will never become ordinary.”

I promised, children. I lied.

We became ordinary in the most extraordinary ways. We argued over salt. We counted coins. We took turns being ill. Every winter, the chimney coughed up black feathers, and every spring, your mother planted buttons in the garden, insisting that shirts would grow. Once, one did. It was a pale green shirt with roots in its cuffs and a nest of mice in the pocket. I wore it to the market, and the mice advised me on cabbage.

Your mother laughed for seven days.

Her laughter was not pretty. No, let us be honest with the dead. It sounded like a piano being pushed down a staircase by angels with broken arms. It frightened birds from statues. It curdled milk at twenty paces. I loved it so much I used to hide jokes in her shoes.

When you were born, she opened like a terrible flower.

There was blood, yes. Blood enough to paint the wolves. Blood enough to teach the white sheets shame. But also there were your fists, tiny and furious, punching holes in the air. She held each of you as if you were warm bombs sent to destroy her loneliness.

Perhaps you did.

Perhaps that is what children are: explosions that leave the walls standing.

You want to know how she died. Always the smallest question carries the largest knife.

She died on a Thursday that had forgotten its own name. The doctors came with their silver faces and pockets full of weather. They opened her chest and found a staircase descending into the sea. At the bottom stood a black cow ringing a bell.

The doctors said many important words. I gathered them afterward and put them in a jar, but they grew mold and began accusing one another. So I buried them beneath the lemon tree.

The truth is simpler.

Her body became tired of carrying her.

It set her down.

For weeks after, I found pieces of her everywhere. Her voice slept in the kettle. Her patience clung to the curtain hems. Her anger—magnificent animal—paced inside the wardrobe, chewing holes through my winter coats. One morning I cracked an egg and her eye looked up at me from the yolk.

“Still burning the toast?” it asked.

I threw the pan through the window.

Then I apologized to the window.

Grief makes a fool of architecture.

Children, do not believe those who say the dead are gone. The dead are merely badly distributed. Your mother is in the stubborn drawer that will not close. She is in the bruise on the peach, in the loose tooth of the moon, in the warm dent left on a pillow after no one has slept there. She is in my beard, where she has built a chapel from crumbs.

Sometimes, late at night, she returns without her skin.

Do not be frightened. She wears the darkness instead, buttoned neatly to the throat. She sits beside me and removes her hands, placing them on the table like two exhausted animals. We do not speak. The dead have no need of speech; they already know the ending of every sentence.

I pour her a cup of tea.

She cannot drink it.

Still, the cup grows lighter.

So come closer, my strange little heirs. Let me look at you while my eyes are still obedient. You are taller than yesterday. This is unacceptable, but I forgive you. One day you will become enormous and sad and full of keys that open no doors. One day your own hearts will sprout teeth.

When that happens, remember her.

Remember the woman who stitched bells into your nightmares so she could hear when you were afraid. Remember how she kissed your fevers and burned her lips. Remember that she once carried three of you through a snowstorm inside a suitcase because the road had turned into a tongue and refused to be walked upon.

Most of all, remember this:

She loved you beyond the limits of her body.

And when the body broke, the love escaped.

It is here now, children—under the chairs, inside the walls, dripping slowly from the ceiling.

Open your mouths.

Do not waste it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a short passage of experimental fiction blending grief, parental affection, nonsense metaphors, food imagery, and dark humor. Use ornate, dreamlike language.
counterfactuals.output:
After Mother died, Father kept her laugh in a blue saucepan, simmering it each Sunday with onions, thyme, and one unlucky pear. “Grief needs seasoning,” he said, kissing my forehead as if stamping a letter to the moon.

At night, the house grew antlers. The wallpaper breathed custard. I dreamed Mother returned wearing a gown of silver anchovies, her eyes two warm ovens, her hands soft as unanswered questions. She fed me stars with a teaspoon and complained that heaven had terrible coffee.

Father and I ate her funeral cake for breakfast until it turned green and philosophical. On the last morning, he raised his fork and said, “Your mother would have hated this.”

Then we laughed—carefully, greedily—while beneath the table death licked up the crumbs.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a bizarre funeral elegy spoken by a widower to his children. Include impossible details such as defective tear ducts, iced-tea tears, ball bearings in pudding, and a mother whose beauty remains radiant after death.
counterfactuals.output:
Children, come close to the casket  
and forgive your father’s defective tear ducts.  
The doctor said grief should pour like weather,  
but mine only click behind my eyes,  
two dry faucets full of moths.

Your mother weeps for me instead—  
from somewhere beneath the lilies,  
from that country without clocks.  
I taste her iced-tea tears in the dark:  
sweet, amber, bewildering,  
with little moons of lemon turning in them.

Remember how she warned us  
not to swallow the ball bearings in the pudding?  
How they rolled against our spoons  
like tiny iron planets,  
and she laughed until the windows  
forgot they were glass?

Now the undertaker has powdered her hands,  
but he could not dim her.  
Death has failed at its only occupation.  
Your mother remains radiant—  
more beautiful than morning,  
more luminous than the chandelier  
that once fell upward into the attic.

Do not fear her stillness, children.  
She is merely listening  
to the roots rehearse their black violins.  
She is learning the names of snowflakes  
that fall in summer underground.

When you miss her, set four places.  
Pour the tea. Strain out the stars.  
If the pudding rattles, let it.  
That will be her, rolling homeward  
through the walls, through our sorrow,  
bright as ever, calling us to supper.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a single-paragraph absurdist monologue beginning with “My beloved little billiard balls,” in which the narrator mourns his wife, praises his children’s beauty, and describes domestic life through surreal non sequiturs.
counterfactuals.output: My beloved little billiard balls, your mother has gone where the teaspoons rehearse their silver operas, and I mourn her each morning by buttering the clock and asking the curtains to wear black. Yet how beautiful you are, my children—your eyes like two polite thunderstorms, your cheeks brighter than the mayor’s emergency pomegranate, your hair arranged by invisible violins! We continue our domestic life as best we can: the kettle files its taxes, the sofa dreams of becoming a submarine, and every Thursday I sweep the hallway into a small but trustworthy volcano. At supper, her empty chair recites the alphabet backward while the potatoes applaud; afterward, I tuck you into the cupboard beneath quilts of moonlight and unpaid invoices. Do not fear the refrigerator when it begins speaking French. It, too, misses her. Everything misses her—even the wallpaper has peeled itself into the shape of a widow, and the old umbrella stands by the door, open indoors, waiting for the rain to come home.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce an uncanny, poetic family remembrance in the style of mid-century literary surrealism: affectionate pet names, grotesque descriptions, scrambled eggs, piano playing, a dying mother, and a final image of the speaker enslaved to her cinders.
counterfactuals.output:
We called her Moth-Mama, Sugarbones, our little Queen of Spoons. In the mornings she stood at the stove in her blue slippers, scrambling eggs until they resembled a heap of torn yellow letters. Her hands were beautiful and terrible—two pale crabs, knuckled with moons—while her smile opened too widely, as though a second family lived behind it.

After breakfast she played the piano. The instrument, black and obese, showed its ivory teeth. Beneath her fingers the old songs came limping out, dressed in our dead father’s cologne. We children gathered close: Chickadee, Button, Worm-heart. Every wrong note laid a cold egg in the room.

When she began dying, she grew enormous in our thoughts and tiny in the bed. Her cheeks became empty purses; her breath, a moth beating against a lampshade. Still she called us her dumplings, her sweet mice, her crumbs of heaven. Still her fingers practiced scales upon the blanket, climbing an invisible piano no one else could hear.

On the last night she asked for scrambled eggs. I made them softly, with butter, and carried the plate upstairs. But her mouth had already become a locked little chapel. The eggs steamed beside her while dawn pressed its gray face to the window.

We burned her in the afternoon.

Now I keep the ash jar beneath the piano. At midnight the keys depress themselves, one by one, and the house fills with the odor of butter and singed hair. I rise when she plays. I bow when she pauses. I turn the pages for hands that are no longer there—

her last darling, her soot-child, forever enslaved to her cinders.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
